newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban nickel/cobalt output tops 50,000 tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Cuban nickel/cobalt output tops 50,000 tonnes.

text.p: Cuba has produced more than 50,000 tonnes of nickel plus cobalt concentrates so far this year, a new national record, state media said on Saturday.

The official Communist Party newspaper Granma said the Cuban nickel industry aimed to lift production to 55,000 tonnes by the end of the year, despite recent heavy rains which had fallen in the eastern mining region of Moa.

Exports of nickel and cobalt are the communist-ruled island's third largest source of hard currency, after tourism and sugar exports. They earned Cuba an estimated $300 million to $400 million in 1995.

Foreign investment and credits have breathed new life into the Cuban nickel mining industry, which was badly hit by the collapse of the Caribbean island's trade and aid ties with the former Soviet bloc, previously the main market and supplier of technical inputs to the industry.

Output rose in 1995 to 43,900 tonnes, sharply up from 26,362 tonnes in 1994. The previous annual production record of 46,600 tonnes was set in 1989, when economic relations with the former Soviet bloc were still normal.
Granma said one processing plant alone, the Comandante Pedro Sotto Alba, would produce more than 24,000 tonnes this year, above the plant's originally designed capacity limit.

The Comandante Pedro Sotto Alba plant at Moa Bay is jointly run by Canada's Sherritt International Corp., which has a big, vertically integrated nickel/cobalt mining, processing and refining venture with the Cuban government.

As a result of this venture, Sherritt became the first foreign company operating in Cuba to be hit by sanctions applied by the U.S. government under the Helms-Burton law, which was introduced in March. The Moa Bay nickel plant was built and formerly owned by a U.S. company.

Directors of Sherritt were informed in July they would be barred entry to the U.S. under the Helms-Burton bill, which seeks to penalize foreign investors in Cuba judged to be "trafficking" in expropriated, formerly U.S.-owned properties.
Cuba's two other operating nickel plants are wholly Cuban- owned.
